findings.title: should_block? has a read-modify-write race condition on match_count
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? loads the record, increments match_count in Ruby, and saves. Two concurrent signup attempts with the same blocked email can both read match_count = 0, both write 1, losing one increment. More importantly, the save is not atomic and there is no locking; under concurrent load the statistics (match_count/last_match_at) that the feature exists to maintain will be silently wrong. Use an atomic SQL update (e.g. BlockedEmail.where(email: email).update_all('match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now)) or update_counters, and do the existence/action_type check in the same query to avoid a TOCTOU window where a record is deleted between the read and the save.

findings.title: should_block? performs a write (save) during validation, mutating state on every check
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called from EmailValidator#validate_each, which runs inside User validation. Every validation of a user whose email matches a blocked record performs a database UPDATE (incrementing match_count and setting last_match_at), even when the user record is never saved (e.g. other validations fail, or the object is built and discarded). This pollutes the match statistics with phantom hits and means a single signup attempt can increment the counter multiple times (valid? is called in UsersController#create before save, and again inside save). Statistics gathered this way are unreliable, and the write inside a validator is a surprising side effect that can also fail and raise inside validation.

findings.title: Email matching is exact and case-sensitive; blocked emails are trivially bypassed
findings.body: should_block? does BlockedEmail.where(email: email).first with no normalization. User emails are stored via Email.downcase elsewhere in the codebase (e.g. UsersController#change_email uses Email.downcase(params[:email]).strip), but the validator passes the raw value. A blocked address 'Spam@Example.com' stored in blocked_emails will not match a signup with 'spam@example.com' (or with surrounding whitespace), so the block is trivially bypassed by changing case. The lookup should downcase/strip the email (Email.downcase(email).strip) before querying, consistent with how the rest of the app canonicalizes emails.

findings.title: BlockedEmail.should_block? is called even when the email value is nil or malformed
findings.body: validate_each receives `value` without any format check. The User model applies `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?` — but there is no built-in email format validator in this codebase (the old code only checked domain whitelist/blacklist), and more importantly validator ordering is not guaranteed: EmailValidator can run when value is nil (presence failure) or a string with no '@'. BlockedEmail.should_block?(nil) will issue a query with nil and, worse, the domain-regexp path calls value =~ regexp which raises TypeError/NoMethodError on nil. Guard with `if value.present?` before calling should_block? or doing the regexp match.

findings.title: Domain whitelist/blacklist regex is injectable and matches substrings
findings.body: email_in_restriction_setting? builds Regexp.new("@(#{domains})", true) directly from the SiteSetting value after only escaping dots. The setting is admin-controlled, but the regex is unanchored: a blacklist entry 'example.com' matches 'user@notexample.com' and 'user@example.com.evil.org' because '@(example\.com)' matches anywhere in the string. Conversely a whitelist entry 'example.com' accepts 'user@sub.example.com' only by accident of substring matching and also accepts 'user@xexample.com'. The pattern should be anchored to the end of the domain: /@(#{domains})\z/i (or split on commas and compare the domain part exactly). As written, both the blacklist (bypassable) and whitelist (over/under-permissive) behave incorrectly.

findings.title: Replacing validates_presence_of/uniqueness_of with validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true changes error messages and breaks the client contract
findings.body: The old code used validates_presence_of :email and validates_uniqueness_of :email, which produce the standard Rails messages 'Email can't be blank' and 'Email has already been taken'. The new combined `validates :email, presence: true, uniqueness: true` produces the same default messages, but the uniqueness validator now runs even when email is blank (it did before too, actually) — the real contract change is that the previous custom email_validator added the localized I18n.t(:'user.email.not_allowed') message, and the new EmailValidator adds I18n.t(:'user.email.blocked'). The client (create_account_controller.js) reads result.errors.email and result.values.email to push into rejectedEmails. However, the controller change in users_controller.rb now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` — in this Rails version (3.x, given skip_before_filter and render nothing: true) errors.to_hash returns {attribute => [messages]}, so result.errors.email is an array, and the JS checks `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` — an empty array is truthy in JS but a present array is fine; the actual breakage: when the email is blocked, the JS pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails and shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid') — but the server message 'is not allowed.' is more informative and is discarded. More concretely: `user.errors.to_hash` on Rails 3.2 returns a hash of arrays; combined with `values: user.attributes.slice(...)` this leaks the raw attribute values back, which is intended, but the JS only handles the case where errors.email exists — for non-email failures (e.g. username taken) errors.email is undefined and nothing is pushed, which is correct. The genuine regression: the previous behavior returned only `message` with full_messages joined; clients that parsed the message string now get a different shape, and any other consumer of UsersController#create (e.g. the omniauth flows, tests) that expected only {success, message} now receives extra keys — additive, but the errors hash shape (arrays vs strings) is undocumented and the JS truthiness check on an array works only by luck.

findings.title: Error response shape change: errors.to_hash returns arrays, but message still uses full_messages; inconsistent and leaks attribute values
findings.body: The create failure path now returns `errors: user.errors.to_hash` and `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")`. In Rails 3.x, ActiveModel::Errors#to_hash returns {attribute => [msg, ...]} (arrays). The accompanying `message` still embeds full_messages.join("\n"). The JS client checks `result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values` — an array like ["is not allowed."] is truthy so it works, but this is fragile. Additionally, echoing back `values` including the email the user just typed is fine, but returning the full errors hash exposes all validation messages (including password length hints) in a structured form to any client, and the shape (hash of arrays) is not what the JS I18n-based display expects — the JS ignores result.errors content entirely and shows a generic 'user.email.invalid'. The response contract is now internally inconsistent: message is human-readable joined text, errors is structured arrays, and the client only uses errors as a boolean flag.

findings.title: rejectedEmails check is case-sensitive and does not strip whitespace
findings.body: The client-side check `this.get('rejectedEmails').contains(email)` compares the raw typed email against the server-returned rejected value. If the user types 'Spam@Example.com' after 'spam@example.com' was rejected, contains() returns false and the email passes client validation, only to be rejected again by the server — a confusing UX loop. The comparison should normalize case (and whitespace) on both sides, e.g. compare email.toLowerCase().trim() against a lowercased rejectedEmails list.

findings.title: rejectedEmails is populated from result.values.email, but the server may not include values when the failure is not email-related; also the pushed value is never cleared
findings.body: In createAccount's failure handler, `if (result.errors && result.errors.email && result.values)` pushes result.values.email into rejectedEmails. Two problems: (1) result.values.email is the server-echoed attribute, which for a blocked email is the same string the user typed, so this works — but if the server ever returns errors.email without values (e.g. the ActiveRecord::StatementInvalid rescue path returns only {success, message}, no errors/values), the guard correctly skips; however the guard `result.errors.email` is an array — if the email error array is empty (shouldn't happen) it's still truthy. (2) More importantly, rejectedEmails is never cleared when the user changes the email to a different, valid address — but since the check is `contains(email)`, a different email won't match, so that's fine. The real issue: the pushed value comes from result.values.email which is user.attributes['email'] — the raw, non-downcased attribute. If the user retries with the same email but different case, the contains() check fails (see case-sensitivity finding) and the server rejects again, pushing a duplicate entry into rejectedEmails (Em.A allows duplicates), growing the array unboundedly across retries.

findings.title: blocked_emails.email has no length limit and no downcasing; unique index is on raw value
findings.body: The email column is t.string :email with no limit (defaults to 255 in most adapters, but the users table uses string(256)) and, critically, the unique index is on the raw email string. Since BlockedEmail.should_block? does an exact match on the raw value, storing 'Spam@Example.com' and 'spam@example.com' creates two distinct rows and the block only catches one casing. The migration should either add a downcased unique column (e.g. email_lower) or enforce downcasing in the model before_validation, and the lookup should use the normalized form. Without normalization the feature's core guarantee (blocking an email address) is broken by trivial case variation.

findings.title: No test for case-insensitive matching or for the write-during-validation side effect
findings.body: The BlockedEmail spec covers default action_type, nil last_match_at, should_block? true/false, and match_count increment, but never tests that 'BLOCK@spamfromhome.org' matches a record created with 'block@spamfromhome.org' — the exact bypass described above. It also never tests that should_block? is safe to call with nil or a non-email string. Given the model performs a save inside should_block?, a test asserting the counter increments exactly once per signup (not once per validation pass) is missing; UsersController#create calls user.valid? and then user.save (which re-validates), so match_count would increment twice per blocked signup attempt — the spec's `change { match_count }.by(1)` only passes because it calls should_block? directly once.

findings.title: EmailValidator spec never exercises the whitelist/blacklist paths and stubs away the real integration
findings.body: The spec only tests the BlockedEmail branch by stubbing BlockedEmail.should_block?. It never tests the email_domains_whitelist or email_domains_blacklist behavior that the validator also implements (moved from User#email_validator), nor does it test that the validator handles a nil value, a value without '@', or that it adds the correct I18n message. Since this validator replaced the inline User#email_validator, the domain restriction behavior — the original purpose of that code — is now completely untested, and a regression in the regex (see the anchoring finding) would not be caught.

findings.title: Email format is no longer validated anywhere; only domain restrictions and blocked-list are checked
findings.body: The old User model had `validate :email_validator, if: :email_changed?` which checked domain whitelist/blacklist but notably did NOT check format either — however the new code replaces it with `validates :email, email: true, if: :email_changed?`, which relies on a validator named `email` resolving to EmailValidator. The new EmailValidator (lib/validators/email_validator.rb) does NOT validate email format at all — it only checks domain restrictions and the blocked list. So `validates :email, email: true` invokes EmailValidator, which never rejects 'not-an-email'. There is no EmailFormatValidator or built-in :email validator in this Rails version, so the `email: true` option either resolves to the custom EmailValidator (which ignores format) or raises ArgumentError for an unknown validator. Either way, syntactically invalid emails are no longer rejected at the model layer — the only format check left is the client-side Discourse.Utilities.emailValid. This is a functional regression: the server now accepts malformed emails like 'foo' (no @) as long as they aren't blocked and no domain restriction matches.

findings.title: Missing trailing newline at end of file
findings.body: The file ends without a newline ('\ No newline at end of file' in the diff). Minor, but it will show up in diffs and some linters flag it.

findings.title: Enum.new is not a standard Rails/ActiveSupport API; actions may not behave as expected
findings.body: The code uses `Enum.new(:block, :do_nothing)` and `BlockedEmail.actions[:block]`. ActiveSupport does not provide a top-level `Enum` class with this interface (there is no `Enum.new` that returns a hash-like object supporting `[:block]` returning a comparable value). Unless the app defines a custom Enum class elsewhere, this will raise NameError at load time, or if some gem provides it, the semantics of `actions[:block]` returning an integer stored in action_type (an integer column) need verification. The fabricator and specs use BlockedEmail.actions[:block] and compare with ==, and the migration defines action_type as integer — if Enum returns symbols, the comparison `record.action_type == actions[:block]` (integer == symbol) is always false and should_block? would never block. This needs verification that Enum exists and returns integers matching the column type.
